Steven Poser's The Misfit, which traces Marilyn Monroe's attempt to heal, through psychoanalysis, the wounds she suffered in her starkly depriving childhood, affords us a rare look at an unusual dyad, a psychoanalytic couple, not generally portrayed as such outside of the sequestered confines of the consulting room. Poser, who is both psychoanalyst and painter, has written on a topic that would seem to be perfectly in his wheelhouse. His artistic sensibility and his ready grasp of the psychodynamics of the case come together in a beautifully rendered account of the ideals and tragic missteps of two highly intelligent, charismatic and talented protagonists.

The reader is confronted with the analyst's predicament when faced with a patient without a cohesive self, who, having suffered a disabling and fragmenting loss of security and self-esteem in her formative years, was desperately in need of care and emotionally unable to function independently; a patient, however, who, despite these deficits (and perhaps in part also because of them)

Wrestling with Destiny: The Promise of PsychoanalysisLucy Holmes. New York: Routledge, 2013. 192 pp.

Stephen Guttman

Stephen Guttman

Stephen Guttman  

Lucy Holmes has accomplished something extraordinary: she has written a book accessible to novices and newcomers to psychoanalytic practice that simultaneously offers insight of value to advanced clinicians. She gives a compelling account of her ideas about how psychoanalysis works and about how and why it has the potential to free us from what appears to be immutable fate. Holmes does this in large part by sharing the frankly emotional essence of her clinical work in the case histories she selects from her extensive private practice. It's a generously passionate book. Because the depictions of the lives Holmes describes and the accounts of what transpired in her consulting room are so engaging and vivid, the book's significant scholarly aspect is easy to overlook, but in addressing issues facing patients, therapists, and society at large, she deftly applies and discusses concepts from a huge range of the literature of neuroscience, medicine, religion, philosophy, literature, and classic and contemporary psychoanalysis.

Roni Ginach   CmTently living in Los Angeles. She completed a master's degree in psychoanalysis at NYGSP in December of 2013. Her thesis, an edited version of which is published in this issue, received both the 2014 Gradiva A ward for best student paper and the Rose McAloon A ward for excellence in a master's thesis. The author explores the genesis of desire as a phenomenon parallel to D. W. Winnicott's theory of clinical fear of breakdown as the fear of something that has in a meaningful sense already occurred, though without our awareness. Desire, in the same way, may be not new but rather a repetition triggered by a sensory reminder of a primitive experience or feeling that is already unconsciously known to us—in other words, has been integrated into our unconscious idiolects early on. Even as the moment of desire emerges, we mourn the loss of the new desired object—as we have mourned the loss of the original object—the devastating experience of separation from the mother in the moment that we gain a conscious understanding, as opposed to an instinctual sense, of self as separate from other/object. This new desire will have taken the form of an attempt at reunification with the original object. Our unconscious knowledge that such a reunification is impossible leads to an inevitable lack of fulfillment and a repetitive cycling, that retraces itself until it finds a home in a new object of desire—which we will learn to mourn in its turn. This topic is approached by means of an analysis of the sculptor Alina Szapocznikow's oeuvre.

[[RunningHead]]

Becoming Freud: The Making of a Psychoanalyst. Adam Phillips, (2014). Yale University Press

Marcus Silverman

Marcus Silverman

Marcus Silverman  

I have long been envious of Adam Phillips. Can there be a more humbling intellectual experience than having a brilliant idea, only to have it pointed out to you that someone else did it first? On a massive scale? And better than you could have possibly imagined? From books like On Kissing, Tickling, and Being Bored: Psychoanalytic Essays on the Unexamined Life (1998) all the way to Missing Out: In Praise of the Unlived Life (2013) and now Becoming Freud: The Making of a Psychoanalyst (2014). His earlier work largely covered the intersection where psychoanalysis comes together with philosophy/ontology, literature, and culture. And he has tackled issues ranging from kindness to tickling to the multifacetedness and hopelessness of choice (in Missing Out), Melanie Klein, Hart Crane, to flatulence, with equal eloquence, originality, and insight. His mastery of language is rare in psychoanalytic (or any intellectually serious) writing today, and with it he manages a truly arduous task, possibly the task, with seemingly very little effort—to make his observations accessible without sacrificing the weight of their substance.

It is perhaps in that spirit then that I imagine he was chosen to write Becoming Freud, part of the “Jewish Lives” series published by Yale University Press to, in their words, “illuminate the imprint of eminent Jewish figures upon literature, religion, philosophy, politics, cultural and economic life, and the arts and sciences. Subjects are paired with authors to elicit lively, deeply informed books that explore the breadth and complexity of Jewish experience from antiquity through the present.” That being said, Phillips doesn't make much of Freud specifically as a Jew. There are some references to the “Jews of Europe at the turn of the century” and resigned framing of Freud's family within the lens of Judaism. It's clear from the start that doesn't interest Phillips much.

[[RunningHead]]

The Examined Life: How We Lose and Find Ourselves. Stephen Grosz, New York: W.W. Norton. 2013.

Charles Lemert

Charles Lemert

Charles Lemert  

The Examined Life was an immediate best-seller upon first publication in Great Britain. A reviewer for the Sunday Times, Robert Collins (2013), said of it that “Grosz's vignettes are so brilliantly put together that they read like pieces of bare, illuminating fiction.” Andrew Solomon (2013), in another blurb on the book jacket, is quoted as saying “impossible to put down.” When first I began to read, I found it quite possible to put down. After the first 30 or so pages, I threw it aside, baffled and irritated.

The next morning I looked up reviews of the American edition. The first to come up was by the New York Times reviewer, Michiko Kakutani, who is the most intelligent and judicious journalistic reviewer I know of. She, too, praised the book, as “an insightful and beautifully written book about the process of psychoanalysis, and the ways people's efforts to connect the past, present and future reflect their capacity to change.” Dutifully, I picked the book up again, and began reading from where I had left off. This time, I couldn't and didn't put it down. And still, for some reason, I resisted writing this review.

Weeks later, when I was ready to write, I reread the book from the beginning. Again, it was a breeze, except for one thing. I discovered why I had thought at first that I hated the book.

Amanda Harris

Amanda Harris

Amanda Harris  

In Poetic Memory: The Forgotten Self in Plath, Howe, Hinsey, and Glück, Uta Gosmann focuses on the ways these four poets make use of “poetic memory,” which she associates to Plotinus's concept of the soul, an entity that possesses more than earthly knowledge. Gosmann compares the poets’ use of poetic memory to the perhaps more culturally apprehensible “historic memory” (which she traces to Plutarch's idea of narrative in identity formation), and she defines her terms (“historic” and “poetic” memory) this way: “What I call ‘historic memory’ presupposes that the self is constituted by the conscious, recollect-able experiences of the past” (p. 1). Further:

Poetic memory, in contrast, posits that the self is more than the compound of a person's remembered biography. Poetic memory does not depend on the accuracy, linearity, causality, or coherence of historic memory, and it reaches beyond the accountable facts of a life toward the notion of a self that is dynamic, expansive, and full of potential. (p. 1)

Margaret Zellner   Licensed psychoanalyst in private practice in New York, a behavioral neuroscientist, and a neuropsychoanalytic educator. She is the executive director of The Neuropsychoanalysis Foundation in New York City, and editor of the journal Neuropsychoanalysis. Zellner is an adjunct faculty member of The Rockefeller University, where she teaches neuroscience to psychotherapists.

This article discusses the neural systems thought to be involved with some of the processes implicated in the repetition compulsion: drives, wishes, and impulses; emotional and reward learning; and self- and affect-regulation. The author looks at the neurobiological underpinnings of these processes and finds that the compulsion to repeat may represent a variety of ways that we try to approach pleasure and avoid unpleasure—which would place it within, rather than beyond, the pleasure principle. The author then suggests some possible mechanisms by which reflecting on the repetition compulsion from a neurobiological and psychodynamic framework may facilitate change.

This paper presents some Lacanian ideas on the repetition compulsion, which Lacan referred to both as the “repetition automatism” (using the older French psychiatric phrase), and as “the insistence of the signifying chain.” At the moment of entering language as Symbolic, the human being is “subject” to the chains of signifiers in the flow; it is indeed the effect of these signifiers. The history of this subject begins at the moment of its insertion into this chain and its fate is in effect sealed. Psychoanalysis can bring about a shift in the subject's position toward the Other such that the subject of speech can claim that fate as its own, can assume the Other's desire as its own, and thereby “choose” to be what it is by fate.

This article discusses the difficulty of establishing and maintaining emotional presence and connection when analysts work with their own difficulties of aging, illness and the prospect of death. In such situations the analyst is caught between the need to care for him or herself, as well as attending to the treatment needs of the patient. In this effort the analyst is challenged by the demands of heightened transferential inductions, as well as the stimulation of multiple subjective countertransferential states. The course can be an uncertain one and the angst which is so often inherent in such circumstances can be experienced as an intolerable darkness of night. Mitigating that darkness requires skill, fortitude, the help of others and the capacity for transcendence.

Reaching the Repetition Compulsion**

Lucy Holmes PHD LP

Lucy Holmes

55 Central Park West Apt. 1F
New York, NY 10023
Phone: (212) 535-9830
Modern Psychoanalysis

Lucy Holmes   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. A former president of The Society of Modern Psychoanalysts, she is a training analyst and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, and The Center for Group Studies. Dr. Holmes lectures throughout the country and is the author of numerous articles on female development and group psychotherapy. Her first book The Internal Triangle, came out in 2008, and her second book Wrestling with Destiny: The Promise of Psychoanalysis was published in 2013.

The author considers the repetition compulsion from a neuroscientific perspective and discusses why it is so resistant to analytic intervention. She argues that the evolved, emotionally charged talking that occurs in the psychoanalytic process can reach the level where the repetition compulsion resides. It can alter the chemistry and structure of the brain in a way that helps patients give up their repetitions and take charge of their lives. Modern analysts favor emotional communication over didactic interpretations precisely in order to reach those deeper, more primitive parts of the brain.

Women Therapists and Resistance to Erotic Countertransference

Nancy Kelly PHD LCSW

Nancy Kelly

4103 Marathon Blvd.
Suite 100Y

NW_Kelly@MSN.com

Nancy Kelly   Private practice in Austin, Texas, as a psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapist. She holds a doctorate in modern philosophy from Stanford. She has trained extensively in modem psychoanalytic group work and has recently joined the faculty at The Center for Group Studies in New York. Dr. Kelly also serves currently on the board of directors of the American Group Psychotherapy Association.

This article arose out of the author's conversations with female colleagues and supervisees, and explores the constriction many female therapists feel in their capacity to have sexual thoughts and feelings in their clinical work. It offers a number of potential explanations, cultural as well as intrapsychic, for women therapists' resistance to erotic countertransference with male patients, and provides clinical vignettes that illustrate some of the ways resistance to erotic feelings may show up in the clinical hour.

The Value of Enactments

Lynne Laub PSYD LP

Lynne Laub

15 West 12th St., Apt. 1B
New York, NY 10011
Phone: 212-929-4811
Email: lynnelaub@aol.com

Lynne Laub   Faculty member, training analyst, and supervisor at CMPS and NYGSP, where she is also codirector of admissions and mi committee miistic director. She has been in private and group practice for 30 years and has published several papers on modern psychoanalysis, including “From Symbolic Communication to Narcissistic Transference,” The Narcissistic Defense-A Protection For Marriage,” “Emotional Attunement,” and “Intuitive Listening.”

Modern psychoanalytic theory and experience tell us that unless the analyst becomes involved enough in the treatment relationship to generate unintended emotional events, the analysis will not succeed. That the analyst will be drawn into the analysand's world through enactments, as well as by other means, presents us with a pathway to understanding the unconscious of the analysand, as well as that of the analyst. Enactments will dislodge the analyst from the traditional position of the objective blank screen. By examining the concept of enactments we can learn how subjective reactions can best be utilized in the clinical setting.

Externalizing the Wish for the Secure Base in the Modern Analytic Group

Aaron Black PHD

Aaron Black

1577 South Ave.
Rochester, NY 14620
Phone: (585) 271 1850
Email: aeblackphd@yahoo.com.

Aaron Black   Received his doctorate from the University of Rochester and is a graduate of the Center for Group Studies training program in New York City. Dr. Black is a clinical member of the American Group Psychotherapy Association and serves on the board of the Group Foundation. In addition, he serves on the boards of the Rochester Area Group Psychotherapy Society and the Group Division of the New York State Psychological Association, where he is also past-president. He has taught, lectured and published papers on psychological trauma, motivation theory, attachment theory, and modern group psychoanalysis. Dr. Black maintains a private practice for individual, couples, and group treatment in Rochester, New York.

The author maintains that the modern psychoanalytic technique of joining to resolve resistances to progressive emotional communication can be understood with reference to attachment theory as stimulating the wish for secure attachment, which is seen as a critical maturational need. Here, the author presents a case example that illustrates how successful joining simultaneously resolves resistance-conceptualized as a symptom of insecure attachment—and arouses attachment dynamics. Aspects of attachment theory and motivation theory are reviewed to suggest that joining techniques in group treatment are especially effective when attachment-related intrapsychic conflicts are stimulated and worked through within the transference.

Revisiting the Repetition Compulsion: Danger and Survival in Early Mental Functioning**

Mary Shepherd PsyaD

Mary Shepherd

36 Hawthorn Street
Cambridge, MA 02138
Phone: (617) 547-2336
Email: maryshepherd@comcast.net

Mary Shepherd   Training and supervising analyst and a faculty member at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. She has written on psychoanalytic research, the anaclitic countertransference, and the relationship between psychoanalysis and biology. Using biological and psychosocial data, Dr. Shepherd conducted empirical research that tested Hyman Spotnitz's hypothesis on the etiology of schizophrenia. Her paper, “Speaking the never spoken: the challenge of id analysis,” won the 2013 Gradiva Award for best article in psychoanalysis. She is in private practice in Cambridge and Brookline, Massachusetts.

The author explores some of the biological and preverbal explanations of the powerful recalcitrance of negative resistant states. Patients come to us for relief or for help with something in their current lives, but gradually slide into a pattern of behaviors and feeling states that we experience as repetitive, and recognize as being repetitive of older patterns. They cling to destructive behaviors and to agonizing feelings, and insist (consciously or unconsciously) that nothing can change. The author suggests approaches for resolving them.
